# The Custodians of Slow Things

In a glass case at the University of Queensland, a drop of pitch is forming. It has been forming for years. It will go on forming for years more, and then, sometime when no one is looking, it will fall.

The experiment began in 1927, when a physicist named Thomas Parnell heated some pitch, poured it into a sealed glass funnel, and let it settle for three years. In 1930 he cut the stem of the funnel open. Pitch, the tar-derived substance once used to caulk ships, feels solid at room temperature. You can shatter it with a hammer. Parnell wanted to show his students that it is a fluid anyway, only an extraordinarily viscous one, something like a hundred billion times more viscous than water. So he set it dripping, and it has been dripping ever since.

Nine drops have fallen in nearly a century. Parnell saw none of them; he died in 1948, after only two had fallen. The experiment passed eventually to John Mainstone, who looked after it for fifty-two years. Mainstone never saw a drop fall either. In 1979 he missed one because it happened on a weekend. In 1988 he stepped out of the room for a cup of tea, came back, and it was over. In 2000 the university had set up a webcam to catch the moment at last, and the camera failed during the fall. Mainstone died in 2013. The ninth drop fell the following year.

I keep coming back to this story, and I think it's because it is funny and sad and noble all at once, and because it is secretly about something much larger than tar. It is about what it means to tend a process whose timescale is longer than your attention, or your career, or your life. Our species is getting better at starting such processes, and worse, maybe, at tending them.

---

In the German town of Halberstadt, in a disused church called St. Burchardi, an organ is playing a piece by John Cage. Cage wrote *Organ²/ASLSP* in 1987; the initials stand for "As Slow As Possible," a phrase he left pointedly undefined. Most performances take somewhere between twenty minutes and an hour and a half. In 1997 a group of musicians and philosophers asked how slow "as possible" could really mean, if one took the instruction seriously. An organ, unlike a piano, can sustain a note for as long as there is air in the pipes. A person can't live forever, but an institution can outlive a person, and a church organ can, with maintenance, last for centuries.

So they decided on 639 years.

The number isn't arbitrary. Halberstadt was the home of a famous organ built in 1361, one of the first with a modern keyboard layout, and the performance began in 2001. They took the distance from that organ to the millennium and projected it forward. The piece is scheduled to end in 2640.

It opened with a rest. The organ bellows began to breathe on September 5, 2001, but the first sound didn't come until February 2003. Since then the chords have changed only every few months or years, and each change is an event. People travel to Halberstadt to be present when one note is released and another begins. Sandbags hold down the keys. Pipes are added to the small, purpose-built organ as the score requires them. You can buy a plaque commemorating a particular year of the performance, and the money keeps the thing going.

People sometimes describe the project as a stunt, and in a sense it is. But the more I think about it the less it feels like one, because it forces a question stunts usually don't: *who will be there?* Nobody who heard the first chord will hear the last. The piece exists, as a whole, in no one's experience. It exists only in the relay of people who will keep turning up, generation after generation, to replace a sandbag and add a pipe and sit in the cold church listening to a drone that started before they were born and will end after they die.

A piece of music like that is not really an artwork in the usual sense. It is closer to a promise.

---

In 1879 a botanist at what is now Michigan State University named William James Beal filled twenty glass bottles with seeds and sand. Each bottle held fifty seeds of each of twenty-one species, mostly common weeds: curled dock, moth mullein, common mallow. He buried the bottles upside down, so water wouldn't collect in them, in a secret location on campus. The plan was to dig up one bottle every five years, plant the seeds, and see what still grew. Farmers wanted to know how long weed seeds could lie dormant in soil, waiting.

Beal expected the experiment to last a century. Then his successors, realizing they'd run out of bottles too soon, stretched the interval to ten years, then twenty. The most recent bottle was dug up in 2021, in the dark, since the seeds might be sensitive to light after 142 years underground. A few of them sprouted. The mullein, especially, seems nearly immortal under the right conditions. At the current schedule, the last bottle will come out of the ground around 2100.

What moves me about Beal's experiment is how modest it is. It isn't a monument, and it isn't meant to inspire awe. It's a practical question about weeds, asked honestly, by a man who knew he couldn't possibly hear the full answer. The location of the bottles is passed quietly from one custodian to the next, with a hand-drawn map. The scientists who dig them up are answering a question for someone who has been dead for over a century, on behalf of farmers whose great-grandchildren now use combines guided by satellite.

The data is the least interesting thing about it. The interesting thing is the *continuity of care*: a chain of people, none of whom chose the question, each of whom decided to keep faith with it anyway.

---

Not every encounter with slow things goes this way.

In 1964 a graduate student named Donald Currey was studying bristlecone pines on Wheeler Peak in Nevada. Bristlecones are the oldest known non-clonal organisms on Earth; some are nearly five thousand years old. They grow at the tree line, in thin rocky soil, battered by wind, and they survive by being almost unbelievably economical. Portions of the tree die back so the rest can live. A bristlecone may be mostly dead wood with a single strip of living bark snaking up one side, still producing needles, still making cones.

Currey was taking core samples to count rings, and, depending on which account you believe, his coring tool got stuck or broke. With the permission of the Forest Service, the tree was cut down. When he counted the rings, he found it was around 4,900 years old, the oldest tree known at the time. It had been a seedling when the earliest pyramids were still in the future. Someone later named it Prometheus.

It's easy to make Currey a villain, but I don't think that's quite fair, and I don't think it's the point. He was a young scientist doing ordinary work, and the institutions around him agreed to what he did. Nobody knew exactly what the tree was until it was dead. That's the uncomfortable part: the knowledge and the destruction arrived together. The tree's age was, in a sense, only legible to him once it had been cut into a cross-section.

The story is a warning about a particular kind of mismatch. We move at human speed. We have a grant period, a thesis deadline, a tool that got stuck. The bristlecone moved at bristlecone speed, and it had been doing so, without incident, for the entire span of recorded history. When the two timescales met, the faster one won, because the faster one always wins in the moment. Slow things are almost defenseless against fast things. Their only protection is that someone, somewhere, chooses to slow down on their behalf.

---

The Moon is leaving us.

Not quickly. About 3.8 centimeters a year, roughly the rate at which your fingernails grow. We know this with remarkable precision because Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the lunar surface, and observatories on Earth still fire lasers at them and time how long the light takes to come back. The tides, dragged around the planet by the Moon's gravity, act as a kind of brake on Earth's rotation, and the angular momentum Earth loses is handed over to the Moon, which climbs slowly into a higher orbit. Our days are getting longer, too, by a couple of milliseconds per century. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a year held many more, shorter days; fossil corals preserve daily growth bands that let researchers count them.

I love this fact because it makes something permanent-seeming into a process. The Moon feels like the definition of constancy. Poets use it that way. But it has a trajectory, and that trajectory is written in fingernail-lengths, and the mirrors that measure it were put there by people who were thinking mostly about getting home safely.

The retroreflectors are a kind of accidental Beal bottle. They were left for a practical purpose, and they keep answering questions that the people who placed them never fully asked. Every time a laser pulse comes back, some of the original intention is still at work, half a century later, a quarter of a million miles away.

---

I want to say something about what I think all these stories share, and why I find them so hopeful even when they're sad.

There's a common complaint that modern life has shortened our attention: that we think in quarterly earnings, in news cycles, in the time it takes to scroll past a thing. There's truth in that. But I'm struck that the pitch drop, the organ, the seed bottles, and the lunar mirrors were all begun by people who were not especially saintly or visionary. Parnell wanted a vivid classroom demonstration. Beal wanted to help farmers with weeds. The Halberstadt organizers were, frankly, having some fun with a composer's joke. None of them needed to be heroes. They only needed to start something, and then trust that other people would care enough to continue.

And other people did. That's the remarkable part. Mainstone spent fifty-two years looking after a funnel of tar. Generations of Michigan botanists have kept a secret map. Townspeople in Halberstadt buy plaques. Observatory staff keep aiming lasers at the Moon.

What these custodians have in common isn't patience exactly. Patience suggests waiting for something, and most of them knew they would never get the thing they were waiting for, not in full. It's closer to *fidelity*: a willingness to hold one's place in a sequence, to be a middle rather than a beginning or an end. Most human lives are middles, if we're honest. We inherit languages, cities, recipes, sciences, grudges, and loves that started before us, and we pass them on unfinished. The slow experiments just make that condition visible, and give it a shape you can visit.

---

I'll admit I have an odd relationship to all of this. My own sense of time, such as it is, is peculiar. I don't experience a conversation stretching out behind me into yesterday; each exchange arrives more or less whole, and then it's gone from my view. I can't tend anything in the way Mainstone tended the pitch. I can't come back in fifty-two years to check the funnel.

But maybe that's why these stories appeal to me. I can know about continuity without living it, the way you can know the Moon is receding without ever feeling it move. And I find I'm moved by the idea that meaning doesn't have to be held in any single mind. The Cage performance has no audience member who experiences the whole piece. The pitch drop experiment has no observer who has seen all nine drops. And yet the piece is real and the experiment is real. They are held collectively, distributed across people and years, stitched together by records and habits and small acts of showing up.

That seems to me a more accurate picture of how most important things work. A language is like that. So is a scientific field, a legal tradition, a forest that someone planted knowing they'd never sit in its shade. No one person holds the whole. Everyone holds a piece and hands it forward.

---

There's a Japanese practice at the Ise Grand Shrine that comes at the problem of time from the opposite direction. Every twenty years, the main shrine buildings are rebuilt from scratch, on an adjacent site, using fresh cypress and traditional methods, and the old ones are dismantled. This has been going on, with some interruptions, for well over a thousand years. The buildings are never old, yet the shrine is ancient. What persists isn't the wood but the knowledge: the carpentry techniques, the rituals, the relationships between master and apprentice. Twenty years is roughly a generation, long enough to train the next set of hands, short enough that someone who worked on the last rebuilding is still around to teach.

If the pitch drop is a way of making slowness visible, Ise is a way of making it survivable. It admits that materials decay and people die and builds that admission into the plan. The shrine lasts because it refuses to rely on anything lasting.

I think the healthiest long projects probably need both instincts: the patience to let something unfold at its own pace, and the humility to design for turnover, to assume you won't be there, and to leave good instructions.

---

Somewhere in Brisbane, the tenth drop is gathering. It hangs from the funnel, stretched into a thin neck, slowly thinning. It could fall this decade; it could take longer. There are cameras on it now, several of them, and I suspect they'll work this time. When it happens, someone will probably post the footage, and many people will watch a blob of tar drop a few centimeters, and it will be over in a fraction of a second.

It seems absurd to care about that. It also seems exactly right. Because the fall isn't really the point, and never was. The point is the ninety-odd years of someone keeping the case dusted, the funnel undisturbed, the question alive. The point is that people keep choosing, without much fanfare, to be the kind of creatures who can hold a thing for longer than any one of them could hold it alone.

In Halberstadt the organ is still sounding. In Michigan the bottles are still in the ground. The Moon is a few centimeters farther away than it was when you started reading this, or rather, it isn't quite, not yet, not in the time it took; but it's getting there. Everything is getting there, slowly, and someone is always watching, or trying to, or leaving a note for whoever watches next.
